title: Infective Bone Disease
path: Management of Clients with Musculoskeletal Problems

headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Infective Bone Disease
headings.content: Infective bone disease, commonly known as **osteomyelitis**, is an inflammatory condition of bone and bone marrow caused by a pyogenic organism. This infection can spread through the bloodstream, from a nearby contaminated structure, or directly through open wounds or fractures. The rigid, enclosed nature of bone makes it uniquely difficult for the body's immune system and standard systemic treatments to clear infections without targeted intervention.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Underlying Mechanisms
headings.content: When pathogens invade bone tissue, they trigger an intense local inflammatory response. This inflammation increases vascular pressure within the rigid bone cortex, leading to thrombosis of local blood vessels. Consequently, areas of bone become deprived of blood supply, die, and separate from the living bone to form a **sequestrum**. The body attempts to wall off this dead bone by producing a new layer of living bone around it, known as the **involucrum**.

headings.title: Etiology and Common Causative Organisms
headings.content:
- **Staphylococcus aureus**: The single most frequent bacterial culprit in all forms of bone infection.
- **Pseudomonas aeruginosa**: Frequently associated with puncture wounds of the foot and among intravenous drug users.
- **Salmonella species**: Commonly identified in patients living with sickle cell disease.
- **Mycobacterium tuberculosis**: Responsible for tuberculous osteomyelitis, frequently affecting the spine in a condition known as Pott's disease.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Patient Assessment
headings.content: Patients with acute osteomyelitis present with systemic signs of infection alongside localized bone pain. The affected area is typically tender, warm, and swollen, with patients often guarding the limb to avoid movement. Chronic osteomyelitis features persistent draining sinuses, low-grade fever, and recurrent flare-ups of pain over many months or years.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Investigations
headings.content: Diagnosing bone infection requires a combination of laboratory tests and imaging studies. Blood work typically reveals an elevated **white blood cell count**, an increased **erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)**, and high **C-reactive protein (CRP)** levels. Plain X-rays often fail to show early bone destruction, as changes only become visible after 30 to 50 percent of the bone matrix is lost. Therefore, **MRI** or bone scans are utilized for early detection, while bone biopsy remains the gold standard to identify the exact causative organism.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: The cornerstone of medical treatment is prolonged antimicrobial therapy, often administered intravenously for weeks followed by oral therapy. Initial antibiotic choices are broad-spectrum to cover likely pathogens like Staphylococcus aureus until culture and sensitivity results are finalized. Pain management, immobilization of the affected limb, and nutritional support to promote wound healing are vital components of the care regimen.

headings.title: Surgical Interventions and Wound Care
headings.content: When antibiotic therapy alone fails to control the infection, surgical intervention becomes necessary. **Debridement** is performed to remove all necrotic bone, infected tissue, and purulent debris. Surgeons may place antibiotic-impregnated beads directly into the bone cavity to deliver high local concentrations of medication, followed by wound closure or management with open packing and vacuum-assisted closure systems.

headings.title: Nursing Care Plan and Patient Education
headings.content: Nurses play a critical role in monitoring neurovascular status distal to the infected site, assessing wound dressings for drainage, and managing breakthrough pain. Patient education must emphasize the critical importance of completing the full course of antibiotic therapy, even after symptoms subside. Nurses also teach patients how to recognize signs of infection recurrence, such as increasing redness, swelling, or fever.
